extracted.intended_audience: general readers and industry stakeholders interested in video game rating policies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Entertainment Software Rating Board's standards, policies, and industry practices for rating, marketing, disclosure, privacy, and labeling of video games (including handling of hidden content, microtransactions, and Adults Only material). Useful for understanding how games are classified, advertised, and regulated in North America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and marketing guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB enforces guidelines adopted by industry to ensure responsible advertising and marketing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines include ensuring game packaging and promotional materials properly display rating information; restricting where promotional materials for games rated 'Teen' or higher can appear; prohibiting publishers from glamorizing or exploiting a game's rating in marketing materials; and requiring online marketing of games rated 'Mature' or higher to be restricted to users who are appropriately aged. These rules are intended to 'restrict video game advertising to consumers for whom the product is not rated as appropriate.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Display and exclusivity of ESRB ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and websites must display ESRB ratings information for games they cover or promote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The board forbids ratings from other organizations from being shown alongside ESRB ratings on publishers' websites or social media outlets. The ESRB Website Council requires online gaming publications to display ESRB ratings information for games they cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online publisher code of conduct (ESRB Website Council)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online gaming publications operating under the ESRB Website Council must follow a code of conduct about rating display and access control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code requires displaying ESRB ratings and implementing systems to restrict access to audiovisual content depicting M or AO-rated games to users who are appropriately aged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trailer and cross-promotion allowances for M-rated games
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB may clear certain promotional uses of M-rated content under specific conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since March 2013, trailers for games that are or are anticipated to be rated 'Mature' can be cleared as appropriate for 'general' audiences (similar to MPAA green band ratings). The board will also, case-by-case depending on the target demographic, allow M-rated games to be cross-promoted in the marketing materials of games with lower ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden/unlockable content disclosure and re-rating policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers must disclose all unlockable or otherwise 'hidden' content as part of the ratings process; undisclosed hidden content can lead to re-rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Hot Coffee and other incidents, ESRB policy (since June 2006) requires publishers to disclose information surrounding all unlockable or hidden content. Games have been re-rated (e.g., M to AO and back) when hidden content was discovered. Publishers can face sanctions, including fines (see Enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and sanctions for misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB enforces compliance and can penalize publishers who misrepresent game content to the ratings board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers can be fined up to US$1 million if found to have misrepresented the content of a video game after further reviews. The board has used swift sanctions in the past, including re-ratings and market removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy certification program (Privacy Certified)
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB offers an online privacy program to help websites and apps adopt privacy policies and data usage practices that comply with relevant laws and best practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program provides 'Privacy Certified' seals indicating certification under ESRB privacy guidelines. In June 2013 the service was extended to mobile apps, emphasizing compliance with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Microtransactions / in-game purchases labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB requires labeling of games that include purchases with real-world currency and specifically labels randomized-purchase mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In February 2018 the ESRB announced a new label for games that contain 'the ability to purchase digital goods or premiums with real world currency' ('in-game purchases'). By April 2018 the label was added to standards. On April 13, 2020 ESRB introduced 'in-game purchases (includes random items)' to apply specifically to purchases with randomized elements (loot boxes, gacha, item/card packs, prize wheels, treasure chests). The original 'in-game purchases' label still applies to other purchase types (DLC, cosmetics, expansions).

rubrics_metrics.name: ESRB stance on loot boxes and gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB's policy position regarding whether loot boxes constitute gambling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In October 2017 ESRB stated that loot boxes were not a form of gambling, describing them as voluntary and comparable to booster packs for collectible card games because purchases guarantee items (though not high-value items). The ESRB added that games containing actual wagering of real money would hold the Adults Only rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downloadable content (DLC) rating maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Downloadable content must maintain the game's original ESRB rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESRB policy requires that DLC not change the original rating; additional or new content in DLC is subject to the same rating considerations and may affect rating requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adults Only (AO) rating consequences and industry acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: AO rating carries significant commercial stigma and distribution limitations within the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AO-rated games cannot be published for major video game console platforms and most retailers do not stock AO-rated games. This dynamic has led to industry self-censorship and efforts by developers/publishers to edit content to obtain an M rating instead of AO. The ESRB has issued AO ratings for extreme content but such ratings are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional recognition and legal enforcement of ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: How ESRB ratings are implemented and enforced across jurisdictions (US, Canada, Mexico).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESRB is officially recognized and used in Canada, Mexico, and the United States. In some Canadian provinces (Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan, and Ontario) ESRB ratings are enforced under provincial law, restricting sale of Mature and Adults Only games to appropriately aged persons. In the US the system is technically voluntary but widely adopted, with some legislative attempts to mandate retailer enforcement (many of which have been struck down as unconstitutional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of content descriptors and transparency concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: ESRB uses content descriptors alongside ratings to indicate reasons for a rating; critics have raised concerns about rating granularity and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content descriptors (e.g., 'Blood and Gore', 'Sexual Content', 'Strong Language') are intended to explain ratings, but critics argue ratings like 'Mature' are too broad (grouping very different games) and that the ESRB sometimes lacks transparency in its ratings process. The board maintains it uses AO when warranted but publishers may edit content to avoid AO due to commercial effects.
